metadata.title: Stock market today: Dow rises, S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline as chip sector tumbles, Nvidia stock falls 6%

content.text:
Stock market today: Dow rises, S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline as chip sector tumbles, Nvidia stock falls 6%
US stocks closed mixed on Tuesday after a blistering rally, as investors assessed what's next for Nvidia (NVDA) and the AI trade now that Jensen Huang is back as CEO.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose nearly 0.9%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 0.5%, bouncing off session lows. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 1.5% after stocks logged their best day since the "Liberation Day" recovery of April 2025.
Tech stocks fell, led by declines in the chip sector. Nvidia shares declined by about 6% following a 31% surge in the prior session. AMD (AMD), Micron (MU), and Broadcom (AVGO) also tumbled.
After paring back bets of a rate hike in December, traders shifted their odds again to forecast a 95% probability that the Federal Reserve will increase rates by 25 basis points and 5% odds of a jumbo 50 basis point hike. The AI rally stoked inflation concerns, while oil prices rallied about 1%.
Several companies released results before the Thanksgiving and Black Friday holidays, including Dollar Tree (DLTR), HPE (HPE), Best Buy (BBY), and Dick's Sporting Goods (DKS). Best Buy shares rose after the electronics retailer posted its best same-store sales growth in five years.
- Ines Ferré
Stocks mixed as Nvidia leads AI trade lower
The major averages were mixed on Tuesday, with shares of AI chip heavyweight Nvidia (NVDA) falling 6%, giving back some of the 31% gains from the prior session amid renewed pressure on the AI trade.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) gained 0.9%, while those on the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) dropped about 1.5%.
149.30 -6.08 (-3.91%)At close: November 25 at 4:00:01 PM EST151.22 +1.92 (+1.29%)After hours: 7:59:59 PM ESTSemiconductor stocks declined alongside other areas of the AI trade as worries about a December rate hike returned to focus.
This will be a shortened trading week, with the stock market open on Wednesday, but closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.
- David Hollerith
Kohl's stock soars after retailer posts sales growth for first time in 4 years
For the first time in four years, Kohl's (KSS) has posted positive comparable sales growth, Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports:
The stock was up 15% by midday Tuesday after the company showcased its turnaround in its third quarter earnings report and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook.
- David Hollerith
Microsoft declares a code red in the middle of a 'Patchpocalypse'
Companies are racing to patch a record number of software flaws this year. Microsoft just found out how long its own fixes take to reach the world, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre writes.
Microsoft (MSFT) has declared a code red, its top-priority alarm, after a 24-hour outage this month, according to internal memos reported by Reuters. The goal is to fix future problems worldwide within an hour. A recent urgent fix took five to six days to reach everyone.
The Nov. 12-13 outage knocked out Outlook, Teams, and Copilot. The culprit was a flaw in Microsoft's own software, introduced in July, that went unnoticed for about four months. Microsoft ruled out hackers and AI agents.
- Ines Ferré
Why Investors need to look beyond Big Tech and embrace bonds in 2027: strategists
The global economy is heading into next year on solid ground, but Franklin Templeton strategists warn investors not to get complacent. With AI giants accounting for nearly half of the S&P 500 and interest rates set to remain high, standard index funds carry more hidden risk than usual, said the strategists in their 2027 Outlook report.
Rather than bailing on the AI boom, the firm suggests investors spread their money across everyday industries such as healthcare and manufacturing that stand to profit from AI adoption.
"Capital is no longer exceptionally cheap. Financing decisions matter more. Valuation discipline becomes essential. And financial resilience increasingly separates winners from losers," wrote Stephen Dover, chief market strategist at Franklin Templeton, and his team.
Meanwhile, higher interest rates mean bonds are finally paying attractive, reliable income again, making them a smart way to balance out a stock-heavy portfolio.
- David Hollerith
US banks' paper bond losses jump nearly 50% in third quarter
The unrealized losses on securities that banks across the country carry on their balance sheet jumped 50% in the third quarter to $486 billion as interest rates surged.
The $159.4 billion increase from the previous quarter came as the nation's total bank loans grew 7.5% from a year earlier— its fastest quarterly pace since the first quarter of 2023, according to new data released Tuesday from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
The FDIC said the banking industry continued to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels, though capital ratios declined during the quarter, in part because of unrealized securities losses.
The nation's 4,205 FDIC-insured institutions earned $84.8 billion in the third quarter, up 7% from a year earlier.
- Ines Ferré
HPE is heading into 2027 with 'tremendous momentum': CEO Antonio Neri
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
HPE (HPE) had the unenviable honor of reporting earnings inside one of the most volatile tech news moments perhaps ever this week.
All things considered, the company handled the moment well — and, importantly, drove home the view that AI demand remains very strong.
"We are entering 2027 with tremendous momentum," HPE CEO Antonio Neri said on Sozzi Unleashed.
HPE is making a pretty compelling case that it deserves to be seen as an AI build-out winner, even if the market may see otherwise for one day.
The company just delivered a strong fiscal fourth quarter, with revenue climbing 50% year over year. Orders surged 88%. The top and bottom lines comfortably beat analyst estimates.
Read more here.
- David Hollerith
Have robotaxis hit a tipping point? Wall Street and experts are split.
If you live in a major city, robotaxis are seemingly everywhere. You've probably seen one, know someone who's ridden in one, or even had a Waymo drive you somewhere. Most people are either enamored or terrified, Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian writes:
But the robotaxi tipping point may be upon us, though there are still a number of hurdles for the industry's major players to surmount before hailing a robotaxi on any US road becomes a reality.
"We're past the tipping point," Anthony Townsend, senior research associate at Cornell Tech and author of "Ghost Road: Beyond the Driverless Car," told Yahoo Finance. "Robotaxis are a technology that has become too big to fail."
But not everyone agrees.
- Ines Ferré
Chip stocks retreat as AI trade comes under pressure
Nvidia (NVDA) stock retreated 7% on Tuesday, giving back some of its 31% surge from the prior session after the board of the AI chip giant reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Peers AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) also declined from Monday's rebound as the overall AI trade came under renewed pressure, as seen on Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace chart.
Shares of memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU) and peer SK Hynix (SKHY) also dropped more than 10%, giving back some of Monday's double-digit percentage gains. Storage and memory players SanDisk (SNDK), Seagate (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) all fell at least 5%.
- David Hollerith
Anthropic's stock price is now less than the price of 'Grand Theft Auto VI'
Was it better to hold exposure to this year's record-breaking IPO or what may be the biggest entertainment launch in history?
The two collided last Thursday when AI giant Anthropic's (ANT) initial public offering hit the market just as Rockstar Games officially released "Grand Theft Auto VI."
So far, the video game trade has come out ahead.
Shares of Rockstar's parent company, Take-Two (TTWO), are up 6% since last Thursday. Anthropic, meanwhile, has fallen below its $83 IPO price and the $79.99 cost of a standard copy of GTA VI.
Take-Two (TTWO) said last Friday that GTA VI churned out $3.79 billion in global sales on its first day, calling the game the biggest entertainment launch in history.
Anthropic's record IPO, which raised roughly $81 billion before any exercise of the underwriters' additional-share option, has quickly shifted from first-day enthusiasm into a tricky debate over how investors should weigh the company's enormous growth prospects against its equally enormous computing costs. Insider share sales and the overall state of the AI trade are other factors for Anthropic investors to grapple with.
The contrast is also a reminder of how quickly the trade around a blockbuster IPO can change. Anthropic's stock climbed 17% in its debut.
Bulls, however, still see a lot to like about the company's future prospects. "I do believe this could be the first $10 trillion company," Madhu Namburi, a managing director at General Catalyst and former veteran tech dealmaker for JPMorgan, told Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa on Monday.
- Grace O'Donnell
Stocks moving on earnings: Dollar Tree, Dick's Sporting Goods, Zoom
Although earnings season has largely wrapped up, investors are still getting a trickle of results from several retail and consumer-facing companies. Here's a look at how some of those stocks are moving in early trading:
Dollar Tree (DLTR) stock popped over 11% after raising its full-year financial guidance and beating earnings estimates once again. As Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports, the budget retailer has reaped the benefits of thrifty shoppers hunting for deals.
Dick's Sporting Goods (DKS) shares surged nearly 15% after beating earnings estimates and increasing its outlook. This was the first full quarter Dick's reported in combination with Foot Locker. On the earnings call, executives said they planned to close more Foot Locker stores and reinvest in others as they work a turnaround playbook.
The J. M. Smucker Company (SJM) also raised its guidance modestly above expectations, but the stock still fell by about 1%.
Zoom Communications (ZM) shares rose 5% after reporting an earnings beat and announcing its first $0.25 quarterly dividend.
- David Hollerith
Stocks fall as Nvidia shares drop and rate hike bets return
US stocks tumbled at Tuesday's open as investors pulled back after Monday's blistering rebound, with Nvidia giving back some of its gains and the return of rate-hike expectations weighing broadly on stocks.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 0.6%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 1.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 1.8%.
50,182.95 +164.25 (+0.33%)At close: November 25 at 4:32:17 PM EST^DJI ^GSPC ^IXICNvidia (NVDA) shares fell after surging 31% Monday following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO. The pullback came as investors reassessed how much further the AI trade can run after stocks posted their strongest day since the April 2025 "Liberation Day" rebound.
- Ines Ferré
HPE stock declines as disappointing margin forecast outweighs upbeat guidance
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) stock dropped 13% in premarket trading on Tuesday after the server and networking products maker reported fourth quarter results.
The company said it expects Cloud & AI operating margins to fall to about 14% in fiscal 2027, down from 18.4% in the latest quarter, raising concerns that pricing tailwinds are beginning to fade.
The outlook overshadowed better-than-expected 2027 revenue guidance and strong order growth. Quarterly cloud and AI revenue grew 68.6% from the same period a year earlier.
Shares of peer Dell (DELL) also fell 7% in premarket trading amid a broader retreat in the AI-related trade. Dell is scheduled to report earnings after Tuesday's market close.
- Jennifer Schonberger
AI market whipsaw puts Kevin Warsh's rate-hike strategy to the test
When stocks tanked last week, Wall Street briefly bet the Federal Reserve would ease up on interest rate hikes. Now Monday's massive rebound — sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia — has revived bets on at least two more interest rate hikes.
Yet with AI stocks still off their highs, the sector's volatility is emerging as a critical test for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the central bank's path for rate hikes.
"AI stress is not mostly due to the Fed. But it is not a coincidence it is occurring when the Fed is hiking," said Krishna Guha, head of central banking and the economy for Evercore ISI. "Talk of 50-basis-point hikes or faster tightening adds to stress. Fed Chair Warsh not talking is a problem. It leaves the market guessing: Is he a hardcore hawk or a market-sensitive hawk? The gap is filled by others whose views can lag the leadership."
"This is a serious test for Warsh," Guha added.
- Brooke DiPalma
Best Buy posts best sales growth in 5 years, stock jumps on raised outlook
Best Buy (BBY) reported third quarter earnings results that blew past Wall Street's expectations in the midst of the most critical shopping season for retailers. The quarterly results marked Jason Bonfig's first as chief executive.
The electronics retailer posted same-store sales growth of 6.1%, its best quarter in five years. Sales growth also surpassed forecasts for a 2.3% gain and the 2.7% growth reported this time last year.
The results were driven by consumers replacing their tech or upgrading to new models. Revenue grew 5% to $10.2 billion, above expectations of $9.9 billion and up from the $9.7 billion posted in Q3 last year. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.62, above the expected $1.49 and well ahead of the $1.40 reported a year ago.
"Disciplined execution, a compelling product cycle and continued market share gains helped drive broad-based topline momentum across nearly all product categories," Bonfig said, which gave the retailer confidence to raise its guidance.
Best Buy stock rose by 5% before the bell on Tuesday.
- David Hollerith
Anthropic's stock slips below IPO price
Only three days after its blockbuster public listing, shares of AI lab Anthropic (ANT) briefly slipped in Tuesday's premarket below its IPO price of $83 per share.
The stock of the Claude model maker fell as much as 6% early Tuesday, trading at $82.30 as of 6:30 a.m. ET before recovering some of those losses. The move comes after the stock market's newest AI giant missed out on a Monday rally that came as chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Anticipation around Anthropic's enormous capital needs and its yet-to-be-shared credit rating, a potential stock supply overhang from insider selling, and ordinary post-IPO profit-taking are all reasons for the lackluster performance, according to Needham analysts.
- Grace O'Donnell
How fear of AI displacement is fueling a hiring recession
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes in today's Morning Brief newsletter:
The US labor market has proved remarkably resilient in the post-pandemic era. But as anyone looking for a job can tell you, it's rough out there. Just getting your resume past AI screeners and in front of a real person is a small victory in itself.
What's been described as a hiring recession is a labor market that has low unemployment but also one that has settled into a low-hire, low-fire environment. One of the reasons workers are staying put and fewer people are being welcomed aboard is artificial intelligence.
After a surge in people quitting their jobs or switching careers during the pandemic, workers are settling back in. But the lower levels of churn, or workers moving between jobs, are especially evident in industries closer to AI, suggesting a connection between a lack of labor dynamism and concerns around the technology.
"Churn has fallen further below pre-pandemic levels in industries with greater AI adoption and automation potential, as workers increasingly stay put amid rising job insecurity," analysts at Goldman Sachs wrote in a research report published Monday.
- Grace O'Donnell
AI market whipsaw puts Kevin Warsh's rate-hike strategy to the test
Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:
When stocks tanked last week, Wall Street briefly bet the Federal Reserve would ease up on interest rate hikes. Now Monday's massive rebound — sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia — has revived bets on at least two more interest rate hikes.
Yet with AI stocks still off their highs, the sector's volatility is emerging as a critical test for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the central bank's path for rate hikes.
"AI stress is not mostly due to the Fed. But it is not a coincidence it is occurring when the Fed is hiking," said Krishna Guha, head of central banking and the economy for Evercore ISI. "Talk of 50-basis-point hikes or faster tightening adds to stress. Fed Chair Warsh not talking is a problem. It leaves the market guessing: Is he a hardcore hawk or a market-sensitive hawk? The gap is filled by others whose views can lag the leadership."
"This is a serious test for Warsh," Guha added.
- Grace O'Donnell
Good morning. Here's what's happening today.
Economic data: ADP weekly employment change, week ended Nov. 7 (23,750 prior); Philadelphia Fed non-manufacturing activity, November (-23.6 prior); FHFA house price index, month-on-month, September (+0.02% expected, +0.03% prior); Richmond Fed manufacturing index, November (-2 prior); Richmond Fed business conditions, November (-5 prior); Conference Board consumer confidence, November (92.1 expected, 91.7 prior); Conference Board present situation, November (121.3 expected, 120.4 prior); Conference Board expectations, November (73.4 expected, 72.6 prior)
Earnings calendar: Dell Technologies (DELL), Analog Devices (ADI), Medtronic (MDT), Autodesk (ADSK), Workday (WDAY), Dollar Tree (DLTR), HP (HP), Best Buy (BBY), Nutanix (NTNX), Burlington Stores (BURL), The J.M. Smucker Company (SJM), DICK'S Sporting Goods (DKS)
Catch up on some top stories from overnight:
How many ousted founders actually get their jobs back?
Oil holds decline on signs of continuing US-Iran diplomacy
US blacklists Alibaba-owned company in setback to AI ambitions
Elon Musk on his support for Jensen Huang: 'Fair-weather friends are worthless'

But the lower levels of churn, or workers moving between jobs, are especially evident in industries closer to AI, suggesting a connection between a lack of labor dynamism and concerns around the technology.

"Churn has fallen further below pre-pandemic levels in industries with greater AI adoption and automation potential, as workers increasingly stay put amid rising job insecurity," analysts at Goldman Sachs wrote in a research report published Monday.
- Grace O'Donnell
AI market whipsaw puts Kevin Warsh's rate-hike strategy to the test
Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports:

When stocks tanked last week, Wall Street briefly bet the Federal Reserve would ease up on interest rate hikes. Now Monday's massive rebound — sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia — has revived bets on at least two more interest rate hikes.
Yet with AI stocks still off their highs, the sector's volatility is emerging as a critical test for Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the central bank's path for rate hikes.

"AI stress is not mostly due to the Fed. But it is not a coincidence it is occurring when the Fed is hiking," said Krishna Guha, head of central banking and the economy for Evercore ISI. "Talk of 50-basis-point hikes or faster tightening adds to stress. Fed Chair Warsh not talking is a problem. It leaves the market guessing: Is he a hardcore hawk or a market-sensitive hawk? The gap is filled by others whose views can lag the leadership."
"This is a serious test for Warsh," Guha added.
- Grace O'Donnell
